https://www.travelwires.com/where-to-do-.text: Where to Do Yoga in Bucharest: A Guide to Yoga Studios and Classes in the Romanian Capital Published by Travel Wires on September 10, 2026 in Destinations & Tourism , Travel Tips & Tricks • 5 min read Bucharest may be better known for its nightlife, architecture and rapidly changing food scene, but the Romanian capital also has a growing yoga community. Across the city, independent studios offer everything from dynamic Vinyasa and traditional Ashtanga to Yin Yoga, meditation and beginner-friendly classes. For travellers spending a few days in Bucharest, expats settling into the city or locals simply looking for a new place to practise, there are now plenty of options. Here are some of the yoga studios and classes worth exploring in Bucharest. VacăPisică Yoga Studio Located at 39 Cameliei Street in Sector 1, close to Piața Matache and within easy reach of Gara de Nord and Piața Victoriei, VacǎPisică Yoga Studio is an independent studio offering a varied weekly schedule. The studio opened in 2019 and focuses on an accessible, down-to-earth approach to yoga, with classes designed for regular people rather than any particular image of what a yoga practitioner should look like. Its schedule includes Vinyasa Yoga, Ashtanga, Yin Yoga, beginner-friendly sessions, mobility and gentler practices, with classes available at different levels and intensities. New visitors can currently purchase an introductory package of three classes for RON 120, allowing them to try different teachers and styles before choosing a regular practice. Class schedule: https://vacapisica.ro/program/ Altar Altar is another yoga space in central Bucharest, located on Calea Griviței, not far from Piața Romană and the city centre. The studio offers several forms of yoga alongside meditation and other wellbeing practices. Its programme includes styles such as Hatha, Vinyasa and Yin, making it an option for visitors looking for both active and slower-paced classes. Its central location also makes it relatively easy to reach from many of Bucharest’s main tourist areas. Sambodhi Studio Sambodhi has been part of Bucharest’s yoga and wellbeing scene for several years and offers a broader mix of activities beyond conventional yoga classes. Depending on the current programme, visitors can find yoga, meditation, workshops and other practices focused on movement and wellbeing. The studio may particularly appeal to those interested in exploring practices beyond a standard drop-in yoga class. THR – The Hot Room For those who prefer a more physically demanding practice, THR specialises in hot yoga and fitness classes. Practising in a heated room creates a very different experience from a conventional yoga studio, so travellers already familiar with hot yoga may find this one of the more distinctive options available in Bucharest. The studio is also located in Sector 1. What types of yoga can you find in Bucharest? The variety of yoga available in Bucharest has expanded considerably, and visitors are no longer limited to one or two styles. Vinyasa Yoga is widely available and is a good option for those who enjoy a more dynamic practice in which movement is connected with breathing. Ashtanga Yoga follows a more structured sequence and can be found both in guided classes and, at some studios, Mysore-style practice. Yin Yoga offers a much slower pace, with poses generally held for longer periods. There are also Hatha classes, mobility-focused sessions, meditation and classes specifically intended for beginners. Many studios allow students to book individual sessions, so joining a class while visiting Bucharest does not necessarily require purchasing a monthly membership. How much does a yoga class cost in Bucharest? Prices vary between studios, but single-class passes and multi-class packages are widely available. A drop-in class will generally cost considerably less than in major Western European capitals such as London, Paris or Amsterdam, while multi-class packages reduce the cost per session further. Visitors staying in Bucharest for a week or more may therefore find a short package more economical than repeatedly purchasing individual classes. Booking in advance is recommended, particularly for smaller studios where class sizes are limited. Yoga in Sector 1 Sector 1 has become one of the more convenient parts of Bucharest for finding yoga studios. The area covers a large part of northern and central Bucharest, including Piața Victoriei, Aviatorilor and areas around Gara de Nord and Piața Matache. Several independent studios operate within the sector, making it possible to find both traditional and contemporary approaches to yoga without travelling far from central Bucharest. For travellers staying around Piața Victoriei or near Bucharest’s main railway station, studios around Matache and Griviței can also be reached easily on foot or by public transport. Joining a yoga class while visiting Bucharest Most yoga studios in Bucharest operate through online booking systems, and advance registration is increasingly common. Travellers who do not speak Romanian should contact the studio before booking if the class language is important. Many yoga teachers in Bucharest speak English and may be able to accommodate international visitors, but this can vary between classes and instructors. Comfortable clothes are usually all that is required. Many studios provide yoga mats and basic props, although checking beforehand is worthwhile if you are travelling without your own equipment. Whether you are looking for a dynamic Vinyasa class, a structured Ashtanga practice or an hour of slower movement after exploring the city, Bucharest now offers a surprisingly diverse yoga scene. Photograph: Darren England/AAP View image in fullscreen Both parties in Queensland have backed formation of a police integrity unit to investigate complaints against police but progress has stalled. Photograph: Darren England/AAP Queensland Queensland anti-corruption commission investigated just 20 of more than 6,000 complaints in a year Statistics showed there is ‘almost no chance’ a complaint made against a government department like the police would be investigated independently, expert says Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Andrew Messenger Mon 28 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Queensland’s anti-corruption commission has investigated just 20 of more than 6,000 complaints of suspected corruption in the past year, as the state government comes under renewed pressure to implement a years-late recommendation to end the practice of police investigating police . The statistic was revealed in Queensland’s Crime and Corruption Commission’s annual report, tabled in state parliament on Friday afternoon. It revealed the CCC assessed 6,198 corruption complaints in 2025-26. It referred 4,244 back to the agency concerned, including the police, local government and public service departments. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email University of the Sunshine Coast criminology professor Tim Prenzler said the statistics showed the state was still operating a “discredited” approach, “facilitating misconduct through impunity”. Prenzler was one of the key experts who advised the landmark 2022 commission of inquiry into police responses to domestic violence. The inquiry considered numerous cases of conflicts of interest and lack of independence in police investigations of its officers. In one case, a police officer was even tasked with investigating their own actions. Subsequent reporting by the Guardian has also revealed allegations by former police officers that the QPS covered up its own failures prior to domestic and family violence deaths and that in other cases policing failures were never properly investigated . The Queensland government promised to put victims first. But it has buried a report from domestic violence survivors Read more It recommended creating a new independent organisation – known as a police integrity unit – to investigate all complaints against police by May 2024 , as one of its “four highest-priority recommendations”. Both parties of government backed the recommendation, but progress has stalled . Prenzler said the statistics showed there was “almost no chance” a complaint made against a government department like the police would be investigated independently. “From the outside, the CCC looks like a powerful independent agency that will thoroughly investigate all allegations and suspicions of public sector misconduct, protect parties, and provide justice,” he said. “In reality, complainants and whistleblowers will have their expectations dashed as their matter is referred back to the agency involved and they will be doubly traumatised by the process.” He said there was no rational justification for delaying the recommendation. “Setting up the police integrity unit must be amongst the easiest things a government could do.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The state’s police minister, Dan Purdie, said police “have got really robust systems when it comes to complaints about police”. “All of those matters are overseen by the CCC. That’s been the case for a long time, and they review all of those matters,” he said. The CCC assessed 6,198 complaints in 2025-26. It retained 20 for its own investigation. It referred 4,244 to the “appropriate agency’”, with 46 referred subject to CCC monitoring, 375 with a requirement for advice on its outcome, and 3,823 referred without any oversight. It also assessed 1,934 complaints as “requiring no further action”. Asked if the unit would be established by the 2028 state election, Purdie referred the question to the attorney general. Unlike New South Wales’s Icac, the CCC is also responsible for investigating crimes such as murder and rape that don’t involve corruption. The CCC held 16 days of corruption hearings in 2025-26 but more than 100 days of crime hearings, its annual report revealed. The annual report revealed the number of corruption complaints has been steadily increasing, up about 47% in the last four years. DONATE TODAY Does this explain the election of Pope Leo? By Phil Lawler ( bio - articles - email ) | Oct 26, 2026 Editor’s Note: Phil Lawler has posted a retraction of this analysis , citing inaccuracies in the report on which this column is based. Within a month after each papal election, stories begin to appear, claiming to provide the inside story of what happened in the conclave. I don’t take those stories too seriously, and you shouldn’t, either. Whoever provided that inside account (assuming the reporter didn’t make it up) was violating his sacred oath to keep the conclave proceedings secret. If he was so cavalier about his oath, why should you trust what he says? But what happens before the conclave is fair game for reporters. The cardinals (and other influential Church leaders) have informal discussions before the papal election, and while those meetings are private, there are no solemn oaths of secrecy involved. So I’m interested in this report by Francesco Capozza of Il Tempo (the link is to a translation posted by Rorate Caeli , about two dinner meetings in the days before the conclave, hosted by Cardinal Raymond Burke). According to Capozza, the dinner guests included all of the cardinals from the US, along with a smattering of cardinals from other countries. Each of the two dinners also included one of the leading papabile : first Cardinal Parolin, the Secretary of State; then Cardinal Prevost. Capozza reports that the dinner conversations produced a clear consensus in favor of Prevost: This is, I repeat, an interesting analysis; I take it seriously. But I would caution against accepting it as the explanation of Cardinal Prevost’s election, for several reasons: Notice that Capozza says that dinner guests would favor Prevost “from the second scrutiny onward.” He also reports that in the first scrutiny (ballot) during the conclave, the Hungarian Cardinal Peter Erdo led the voting. If that is accurate—again I am skeptical of any report about events during the conclave—it is not clear why a “conservative” bloc would feel obliged to choose between Prevost and Parolin as an alternative. Most Vatican-watchers had rated Erdo a more conservative candidate than either of them. If all of the American cardinals were in attendance at the dinners in Cardinal Burke’s apartment—including Cardinals Cupich, McElroy, Gregory, and Tobin—then these could not be characterized as gatherings of a “conservative” bloc. More likely the prelates were hoping to settle on a compromise candidate, judging that neither a “liberal” nor a “conservative” cardinal could reach the necessary majority. Pre-conclave dinners give the voting cardinals a valuable opportunity to weigh both the merits of the papabile and their potential support. But the results of those discussions are not binding; the participants do not endorse a candidate for the papacy, and each cardinal remains free to cast his own secret ballot as he chooses. There were other such meetings before the 2025 conclave, and cardinals had time to change their minds. A dinner might produce a trend in favor of one cardinal, but it does not guarantee a “package” of conclave votes. Even if the Burke dinners did end in a consensus, a bloc of “between twenty and twenty-five” votes was not sufficient to elect a new Pontiff. It was a substantial bloc, to be sure, potentially a crucial swing vote if the first ballots produced no clear front-runner. Capozza’s sources were obviously cardinals who attended the dinners, and saw them as key factors in building support for Cardinal Prevost. Certainly the discussions would have been key factors in the thinking of those particular cardinals as the conclave approached. Other cardinals may have been swayed—for or against Prevost—by completely different influences. Human nature being what it is, the people who participate in any historic act are tempted to exaggerate their own importance. Finally, I would wager that the cardinals most likely to exaggerate their role in (or before) a conclave are also the ones most loquacious in responding to inquisitive reporters. My conclusion: The Capozza story is entirely plausible, an example of solid journalism, but not a complete account. It has the ring of truth but not the certainty of the Gospel. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/nu-s.text: Donald Tusk a declarat că țările europene trebuie să aibă un cuvânt de spus în orice acord care să remodeleze arhitectura de securitate a continentului. Prim-ministrul polonez a avertizat că Europa nu va permite ca SUA și Rusia să negocieze un acord de securitate „pe la spatele nostru”, pe fondul unor informații conform cărora Washingtonul ar fi solicitat Moscovei să propună un nou aranjament de securitate pentru continent, scrie TVPWorld . Vorbind joi cu reporterii la summitul Comunității Politice Europene de la Dublin, Tusk a subliniat necesitatea implicării europene în orice discuții privind securitatea continentului. „În niciun caz nu vom permite nimănui să stabilească noi reguli de securitate în această parte a lumii fără consultarea noastră - fără consultarea Poloniei și a Europei”, a spus el. „Nu vom construi o nouă arhitectură de securitate doar pentru că președintele rus sau, de exemplu, cineva din Statele Unite dorește acest lucru. Este exclus.” Avertismentul a venit după ce site-ul de știri american Axios a relatat , citând două surse familiarizate cu discuțiile, că administrația președintelui Donald Trump a solicitat Rusiei să prezinte propuneri pentru un viitor acord de securitate cu Europa. Conform articolului, emisarii lui Trump, Jared Kushner și Steve Witkoff, au solicitat Moscovei să-și prezinte cerințele de securitate și să propună măsuri pentru atenuarea tensiunilor cu Europa în cadrul negocierilor de pace mediate de SUA dintre Rusia și Ucraina, desfășurate la Abu Dhabi la începutul acestei săptămâni, care s-au încheiat fără un progres semnificativ. Rusia urmărește de mult timp impunerea unor restricții asupra extinderii NATO și reducerea prezenței militare occidentale în Europa de Est, cerințe pe care Washingtonul le-a respins anterior. Trump a declarat săptămâna trecută că lucrează la un „acord mare și frumos” care ar putea implica întreaga Europă, deși a oferit puține detalii. Pentru Polonia, care se învecinează cu Ucraina și cu exclava Kaliningrad a Rusiei, puternic militarizată, perspectiva unui astfel de acord are o importanță deosebită. Varșovia se află în stare de alertă sporită încă de la invazia rusă din Ucraina în 2022 și a acuzat în repetate rânduri Moscova de sabotaj și alte activități ostile. Între timp, Witkoff a declarat joi că președintele rus Vladimir Putin a fost de acord să permită reprezentanților europeni să se alăture următoarei runde de negocieri de pace privind Ucraina. „Europenii se vor alătura la următoarea întâlnire, moment pe care îl considerăm foarte important, deoarece ei sunt partenerii noștri și este important pentru noi ca aceștia să participe”, a declarat Witkoff pentru televiziunea de stat rusă după întâlnirea cu Putin la Moscova. Ar fi prima dată când reprezentanții europeni se alătură negocierilor de pace mediate de SUA de când Trump și-a lansat efortul diplomatic după revenirea la Casa Albă anul trecut, deși rămâne neclar dacă Moscova este pregătită să facă concesii semnificative în vederea unui acord de pace. Tusk a afirmat că a observat o poziție europeană unitară în această chestiune, adăugând că orice acord de pace trebuie să garanteze că „Ucraina își păstrează suveranitatea și, mai presus de toate, că arhitectura de securitate din Europa de Est rămâne neschimbată”. „Pot spune cu o mare liniște sufletească că nu văd diviziuni interne, nici fisuri, între țările Uniunii Europene”, a spus el. Tusk a recunoscut, de asemenea, că obiectivele diplomatice ale Washingtonului s-ar putea să nu se alinieze pe deplin cu așteptările Europei. „Obiectivele diplomației americane ar putea diferi oarecum de ceea ce așteaptă Europa”, a spus el.
